questions.question: What is the error in a control loop?
options: The setpoint minus the measurement
The difference between two consecutive measurements
How far the output is from its limit
The time between updates
questions.explanation: Error is what you want minus what you have. Every term of a PID controller is a different response to that one number.

questions.question: Why does a proportional only controller settle short of the target?
options: It only produces a command while error remains, so some error must remain to hold position
Because the gain is always too small
Because it ignores the measurement
Because the output saturates
questions.explanation: Holding the robot at speed needs a non zero command, and proportional can only produce one from a non zero error. That leftover is steady state error.

questions.question: What is integral windup?
options: The integral growing without bound while the output is already saturated
The integral term oscillating around zero
The derivative term spiking when the setpoint changes
The integral being reset too often
questions.explanation: When the machine cannot deliver what is asked, error never clears and the accumulator keeps climbing, then takes a long time to unwind.

questions.question: Why compute derivative from the measurement rather than from the error?
options: A setpoint change makes error jump instantly, which spikes the output for one step
Because the error is not available in time
Because measurement is more accurate than setpoint
Because it makes the maths simpler
questions.explanation: The measurement moves smoothly because it is physical. The error can jump the instant an operator changes the target, and the derivative of a jump is enormous.

questions.question: What is the anti windup rule the reference uses?
options: Stop accumulating when the output is saturated and the error pushes further into saturation
Reset the integral every time the output saturates
Clamp the integral to plus or minus one
Divide the integral by the time step
questions.explanation: Accumulation is only paused in the direction that cannot help. Error pushing back towards the usable range still accumulates, so recovery stays quick.

questions.question: What is the usual order for tuning a PID controller on real hardware?
options: Raise proportional until it just oscillates and back off, add derivative to damp, then add integral to remove the offset
Set integral first, then proportional, then derivative
Set all three to the same value and scale together
Compute all three from the plant model and never adjust them
questions.explanation: Tuning is physical. Proportional sets the responsiveness, derivative damps the overshoot it causes, and integral cleans up what is left.
